A paper trail: SeaBrick's patent history

A restrained account of what has been filed, when, and what it does and does not mean.

A nonprofit that wants to set standards has an awkward relationship with patents. On one hand, an open standard works best when anyone can use it. On the other, an idea with no protection at all tends to get fenced off by whoever moves fastest. SeaBrick's approach has been to file, to keep the filings in the hands of the project, and to be plain about what they cover.

The first filing

Patent counsel was engaged in January 2022, and on 10 March 2022 a United States provisional application was filed under the title "Kelp-Based Modular Construction Blocks and Methods of Making Same", with SeaBrick Society as applicant. The founder described the draft at the time as "sixty pages of awesomeness"; it covered the blocks, the compressed-biomass material and the way the blocks join.

A year later, on 10 March 2023, the international (PCT) application was filed through the Canadian Intellectual Property Office. It was published on 14 September 2023 as WO2023168537A1. National-phase applications followed in Canada and the United States in September 2024. In 2023 the Society assigned this family to the related operating company so that commercial development could proceed; the Society's role remained the standard rather than the product.

The 2024 filings

Three provisional applications were filed in early 2024, on kelp farm structures, on methods of making seaweed-based composites (the Kelpstone process developed with UBC), and on a modular, container-sized apparatus for processing biomass in remote communities. They reflect a period when the project believed it would have to build the kelp supply chain itself.

The 2025 filing

On 9 December 2025 a new provisional application, "Modular Construction Blocks and Methods of Making Same", was filed covering the component-based brick design and the current approach to moulding. At more than two hundred pages it is the most complete description of the system to date.

What this does and does not mean

Published applications are public documents; anyone can read them. A filing is not a granted patent, and this page makes no claim about the legal status or scope of any application. Trademark applications for the SeaBrick name exist in Canada and the United States. If you are considering building on the SeaBrick system, write to us; the point of the Society is to make that possible.
